approved_row.title: Compact groups are type I and their direct integrals collapse to discrete Hilbert sums
approved_row.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a compact second-countable group. Then: (1) every factor representation of $K$ on a separable Hilbert space is a multiple of an irreducible representation, so $K$ is a type I group; and (2) every strongly continuous unitary representation of $K$ on a separable Hilbert space is a discrete orthogonal Hilbert sum of copies of irreducible representations, $$\pi\cong\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}m_\alpha\,\pi_\alpha,\qquad m_\alpha\in\{1,2,\dots,\infty\},$$ over the countable set $I\subset\widehat K$ of irreducible classes occurring in $\pi$; in the Peter-Weyl case of the regular representation the multiplicities are the dimensions. In particular the continuous direct integrals of the general theory degenerate to atomic sums for compact groups.
approved_row.strategy: By the published Peter-Weyl theory every unitary representation of $K$ is a direct sum of finite-dimensional irreducibles, equivalently a discrete isotypic decomposition $\pi\cong\bigoplus_\alpha m_\alpha\pi_\alpha$ ([[thm-arbitrary-unitary-representations-of-compact-groups-decompose-discretely]], [[thm-regular-representation-peter-weyl-decomposition]]); the set $I$ of occurring classes is countable because the nonzero isotypic components are pairwise orthogonal closed subspaces of the separable Hilbert space $H$. If $\pi$ is factorial, its generated von Neumann algebra is a factor, and the isotypic decomposition must have a single isotypic component, because the projections onto distinct isotypic components are central in $\pi(K)''$; hence $\pi\cong m\pi_\alpha$ is a multiple of an irreducible. Therefore every factor representation of $K$ is type I in the sense of [[def-type-i-factor-representation-and-type-i-group]], so $K$ is type I. Item (2) is the published discrete decomposition restated. The multiplicities for the regular representation are the dimensions of the irreducibles by the same published theorem.

approved_row.title: Direct integrals of compact groups are atomic Hilbert sums
approved_row.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $K$ be a second-countable compact group with normalised Haar measure and let $(\pi,H)$ be a strongly continuous unitary representation of $K$ on a separable Hilbert space. Then $\pi$ is a discrete orthogonal Hilbert sum of isotypic pieces $$\pi\cong\bigoplus_{\alpha\in I}m_\alpha\pi_\alpha$$ over the countable set $I$ of irreducible classes occurring in $\pi$, each $\pi_\alpha$ finite dimensional and $m_\alpha\in\{1,2,\dots,\infty\}$. This is the direct-integral formalism over the measure space $(\widehat K,\text{counting measure})$: the measurable field has fibres $H_\alpha:=m_\alpha\pi_\alpha$-spaces over the atoms, every atom is measurable, and the integral is the direct sum. In the case of the left regular representation the multiplicities are $m_\alpha=\dim\pi_\alpha$ with the appropriate normalisation, by Peter-Weyl.
approved_row.strategy: Apply the published decomposition of arbitrary compact-group representations into direct sums of irreducibles [[thm-arbitrary-unitary-representations-of-compact-groups-decompose-discretely]], grouping equal irreducible classes into isotypic components to obtain the stated multiplicities; the regular-representation multiplicities are the dimension statement of [[thm-regular-representation-peter-weyl-decomposition]]. The comparison with the direct-integral language is the observation that counting measure on the countable discrete space $\widehat K$ makes every fibre space $H_\alpha$ a measurable field with the direct integral equal to the algebraic orthogonal direct sum; this is the simplest case of Example 1.G.1(1) of the source. No continuous measure occurs, which is exactly the content of the compact corollary.

approved_row.title: The left regular factor of an ICC discrete group is a non-type-I factor
approved_row.statement: Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\Gamma$ be a countably infinite group in which every nonidentity conjugacy class is infinite (ICC), for instance the free group on two generators or the group of finitely supported permutations of $\mathbb N$. Let $\lambda_\Gamma$ be the left regular representation on $\ell^2(\Gamma)$ and $L(\Gamma):=W^*(\lambda_\Gamma(\Gamma))\subseteq\mathcal B(\ell^2(\Gamma))$. Then: (1) $\tau(T):=\langle T\delta_e,\delta_e\rangle$ is a faithful normal tracial state on $L(\Gamma)$ with $\tau(I)=1$, and $L(\Gamma)$ is infinite dimensional; (2) $L(\Gamma)$ is a factor, i.e. $Z(L(\Gamma))=\mathbb CI$; (3) $L(\Gamma)$ is not a type I factor, hence $\lambda_\Gamma$ is a factor representation that is not a multiple of an irreducible representation. Thus the canonical central decomposition of $\lambda_\Gamma$ has a single non-irreducible factor fibre, exhibiting that factor representations need not be irreducible and that the type I hypothesis in the irreducible disintegration theorem is essential.
approved_row.strategy: (1) is the trace computation recorded in [[def-tracial-state-and-faithful-normal-trace-on-a-von-neumann-algebra]]: normality is WOT-continuity of a vector functional; traciality is checked on the $*$-algebra generated by the $\lambda_\Gamma(g)$, where it reduces to $\tau(\lambda(gh))=\tau(\lambda(hg))=\delta_{gh,e}$, and passes to weak-operator limits by separate continuity; faithfulness: if $T\delta_e=0$ and $T\in L(\Gamma)$, then for every $g$ one has $T\delta_g=T\lambda(g)\delta_e=\lambda(g)T\delta_e=0$, and $(\delta_g)$ spans a dense subspace; infinite dimensionality follows because the $\lambda(g)$ are linearly independent ($\sum c_g\lambda(g)=0$ applied to $\delta_e$ and paired with $\delta_{h^{-1}}$ gives $c_h=0$). (2) Let $T\in Z(L(\Gamma))$ and write $T\delta_e=\sum_gc_g\delta_g$. For every $h\in\Gamma$, centrality gives $T=\lambda(h)T\lambda(h)^{-1}$, hence $T\delta_e=\lambda(h)T\delta_{h^{-1}}=\lambda(h)\lambda(h^{-1})T\delta_e$... computing coefficients gives $c_{hgh^{-1}}=c_g$ for all $g,h$, so $(c_g)$ is constant on conjugacy classes; square-summability together with the ICC hypothesis forces $c_g=0$ for $g\neq e$ (conjugacy classes are infinite). Then $T\delta_e=c_e\delta_e$, and for every $g$, $T\delta_g=T\lambda(g)\delta_e=\lambda(g)T\delta_e=c_e\delta_g$, so $T=c_eI$ and the centre is trivial. (3) Suppose $L(\Gamma)$ were a type I factor. By [[lem-separable-type-i-factors-are-multiples-of-irreducible-representations]] it would be isomorphic to $\mathcal B(K)$ for a nonzero separable $K$. If $K$ is infinite dimensional, $\mathcal B(K)$ contains orthogonal projections $p,q$ with $I$ equivalent to $p$ and to $q$ (choose two orthogonal infinite-dimensional subspaces of $K$), so a tracial state $\sigma$ would satisfy $1=\sigma(I)=\sigma(p)=\sigma(q)$ while $\sigma(p+q)=2>1$, a contradiction; if $K$ is finite dimensional, $\mathcal B(K)$ is finite dimensional, contradicting the infinite dimensionality from (1). Hence $L(\Gamma)$ is not type I and $\lambda_\Gamma$ is not a multiple of an irreducible.

approved_row.title: Irreducible multiplicity data is not canonical outside type I
approved_row.statement:
False claim: for every second-countable locally compact group, the irreducible direct-integral data of a representation - the measure class on the unitary dual and the multiplicity function - is canonically determined. Counterexample: let $F=\langle a,bangle$ be the free group on two generators, $A=\langle aangle$, $B=\langle bangle$, and let $\lambda_F$ be the left regular representation on $\ell^2(F)$. Then there are two direct integral decompositions into irreducible representations $$\lambda_F\cong\int_{\widehat A}^\oplus\operatorname{Ind}_A^F\chi\,d\mu(\chi)\cong\int_{\widehat B}^\oplus\operatorname{Ind}_B^F\psi\,d
u(\psi),$$ where $\mu,
u$ are Haar measures on the compact duals $\widehat A,\widehat B\cong\mathbb T$, every fibre $\operatorname{Ind}_A^F\chi$ and $\operatorname{Ind}_B^F\psi$ is irreducible, and $\operatorname{Ind}_A^F\chi
ot\cong\operatorname{Ind}_B^F\psi$ for all $(\chi,\psi)\in\widehat A	imes\widehat B$. Moreover $F$ is not type I, because $L(F)$ is an infinite-dimensional non-type-I factor ([[ex-the-left-regular-factor-of-an-icc-discrete-group]]). Hence the two decompositions have disjoint supports in the dual and there is no uniqueness of irreducible multiplicity data: only the central factor decomposition is canonical.
approved_row.strategy: (i) Realise all $\operatorname{Ind}_A^F\chi$ on the single Hilbert space $\ell^2(A\backslash F)$ by the transversal model $\bigl(\pi_\chi(g)f\bigr)(t)=\chi(\alpha(t,g))f(t\cdot g)$ of [[def-commensurator-unitary-character-and-monomial-induced-representation]]; for fixed $g$ only finitely many $t$ matter on finitely supported $f$, and $\chi\mapsto\chi(\alpha(t,g))$ is continuous on the compact group $\widehat A$, so $\chi\mapsto\pi_\chi(g)$ is a measurable field of representations over the constant field $\ell^2(A\backslash F)$; the direct integral $\int_{\widehat A}^\oplus\pi_\chi\,d\mu(\chi)$ is therefore defined by [[def-direct-integral-of-unitary-representations]]. (ii) The constant section $\xi=(\delta_A)$ has norm one and coefficient $\langle\pi(g)\xi,\xi\rangle=\int_{\widehat A}\langle\pi_\chi(g)\delta_A,\delta_A\rangle\,d\mu(\chi)$; in the transversal model the $(A,A)$-coefficient of $\pi_\chi$ equals $\chi(g)$ if $g\in A$ and $0$ otherwise, so by the identification $\widehat A\cong\mathbb T$ with normalized Haar (arc) measure and the orthonormality of trigonometric characters, $\int_{\widehat A}\chi(g)\,d\mu(\chi)=0$ for $g\neq e$ and $=1$ for $g=e$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]], [[lem-trigonometric-characters-are-orthonormal]]). Hence the coefficient function is $\delta_{g,e}=\langle\lambda_F(g)\delta_e,\delta_e\rangle$. (iii) Cyclicity must be proved globally, not inferred from fibrewise cyclicity. For each transversal coset At choose its right-transversal representative t. In the source convention pi(t^{-1})delta_e=delta_t and pi(a^n)delta_e=chi(a)^n delta_e, so pi(t^{-1}a^n)delta_e=chi(a)^n delta_t. Hence the orbit of xi contains, for each coset, every trigonometric monomial times delta_t, up to one fixed character phase, which only shifts the integer exponent. The trigonometric system is complete in L2(T) by [[thm-trigonometric-system-is-complete-in-l-two-of-the-torus]]. Finite sums over cosets are dense in the constant-field integral L2(T;l2(A\backslash F)): truncate cosets and then Fourier-approximate each scalar component. Thus xi is cyclic. The cyclic GNS uniqueness theorem gives lambda_F equivalent to the integral; repeat with B. This proof uses the actual Fourier basis, not the corrected localization clause as a substitute for orbit density. (iv) Irreducibility: $A$ is self-commensurating in $F$ and $g^{-1}Bg\cap A=\{e\}$ for all $g$, by the free-factor lemma; the Mackey-Shoda irreducibility criterion (with the vacuous hypothesis, since $\operatorname{Comm}_F(A)=A$) makes every $\operatorname{Ind}_A^F\chi$ irreducible, and symmetrically for $B$. (v) Non-equivalence: in the non-equivalence criterion take $H_1=A,H_2=B$; every intersection $g^{-1}Bg\cap A$ is trivial and hence of infinite index in the infinite group $A$, so the hypothesis is vacuous and $\operatorname{Ind}_A^F\chi\not\cong\operatorname{Ind}_B^F\psi$ for all $\chi,\psi$. (vi) The two decompositions therefore use pairwise non-equivalent irreducibles throughout, so no choice of measure class on $\widehat F$ together with a multiplicity function can represent both; and $F$ is not type I by the ICC example together with [[def-type-i-factor-representation-and-type-i-group]] (a type I group has every factor representation a multiple of an irreducible, which fails for $\lambda_F$). This is Example 1.G.11(1) of the source, with the equivalence of the integrated representations proved here by the GNS argument rather than quoted. The dual of the cyclic free factor is identified with the circle locally: a character is uniquely determined by chi(a)=z in the unit circle and has chi(a^n)=z^n; compact-open topology on the discrete cyclic group agrees with this evaluation topology because its compact subsets are finite. Transport the A-page normalized circle Haar integral through this homeomorphism. The orthonormality theorem supplies the integral of z^n, and the A-page Fourier completeness theorem supplies cyclicity. No B-homed published example is a prerequisite.
